Challenging Your Thesis: The "Cleanest Dirty Shirt" Paradox
As your trading peer, I will play devil's advocate. While your long-term math is unassailable, the market can remain irrational longer than an investor can remain solvent. Here is where your thesis could face structural friction:
1. The Paradox of Relative Currency Strength
The U.S. dollar does not trade in a vacuum; it trades against a basket of other fiat currencies (like the Euro, Yen, and Pound). Even if the U.S. fiscal situation is deteriorating, the Eurozone, Japan, and the UK face even worse demographic and debt-to-GDP profiles. [1]
The Trading Reality: If global capital perceives every other country as being in worse financial shape, money will continue to flood into U.S. Dollars and Treasury bonds purely as a defensive haven. The dollar can continue to strengthen globally even while expanding its money supply, suppressing gold prices for years. [1, 2]
2. The High-Yield Capital Strike
If the Fed keeps rates at today's restrictive levels to combat M2-driven inflation, nominal yields on U.S. Treasuries will remain high (e.g., 4% to 5%).
The Trading Reality: Institutional money managers operate under strict mandates. When safe, risk-free government bonds yield 5% in a highly volatile global market, large pension and sovereign wealth funds will choose guaranteed cash yield over a non-yielding asset like physical gold, drying up the speculative inflows needed to drive gold to new highs.
3. Technology and Productivity Distortions
A massive historical blind spot for commodity investors is a sudden, macro-shifting productivity boom.
The Trading Reality: If rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), robotics, and automation trigger a severe deflationary wave by drastically lowering the cost of goods and services, the Fed's M2 expansion will be naturally absorbed. Productivity-driven deflation would allow the Fed to lower interest rates without triggering inflation, completely dismantling the "currency debasement" trigger for gold.
Global Currencies: The Ripple Effect of a Static Fed
If the U.S. Federal Reserve maintains interest rates at today's roughly 5.00%–5.25% benchmark baseline for an extended period, it forces the rest of the world into an incredibly difficult economic box. Here is how major foreign blocks are likely to react:
                      ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐

                      └─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                            │
               ┌────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┐

  ┌─────────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │     EUROZONE & UK       │  │          JAPAN          │  │    EMERGING MARKETS     │
  ├─────────────────────────┤  ├─────────────────────────┤  ├─────────────────────────┤

  │ Result: Weak EUR/GBP,   │  │ defend Yen.             │  │ Result: Devalue fiat,   │
  │ imported inflation.     │  │ Result: Domestic crash. │  │ sell gold for USD.      │
  └─────────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘
1. The Eurozone and United Kingdom: Forced Depreciation
Both the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of England (BoE) are dealing with much weaker domestic growth profiles than the U.S. If they keep their interest rates high just to match the Fed, they risk plunging their heavily indebted southern European members (like Italy and Greece) into a severe banking crisis.
The Action: They will likely be forced to cut interest rates ahead of the Fed.
The Impact: This will cause the Euro (EUR) and British Pound (GBP) to sharply depreciate against the USD. A weaker Euro makes imported energy and commodities more expensive, creating "imported inflation" across Europe. [1]
2. Japan: The Endgame Crisis
Japan is the most vulnerable node in this matrix. With a debt-to-GDP ratio breaching 260%, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) cannot raise rates significantly without bankrupting its own government. However, if the Fed stays high, the interest rate differential will continue to obliterate the Japanese Yen (JPY). [1]
The Action: The BOJ will be forced to aggressively deploy their massive U.S. Treasury reserves to artificially buy and defend the Yen, or be cornered into capitulatory rate hikes that shock their domestic bond market.
The Impact: Extreme global bond market volatility, which historically triggers systemic liquidations where gold miners get caught in the initial crossfire.
3. Emerging Markets (EM): Defending Against Capital Flight
When U.S. yields remain high, global capital leaves emerging markets (Latin America, Southeast Asia) and flows back to Wall Street to capture high risk-free returns.
The Action: To stop their currencies from collapsing, EM central banks must either raise their own interest rates to economically painful levels, or liquidate their physical gold and USD reserves (much like Turkey did) to defend their local currencies.
The Impact: This creates localized, recurring waves of physical gold supply hitting the market, acting as a near-term ceiling on the commodity price despite the long-term bullish setup.
Hidden Indicators for Your Dashboard
To track if your thesis is playing out cleanly or getting disrupted by these global forces, add these three key indicators to your daily screening routine:
The Cross-Currency Basis Swap: Watch the premium foreign banks pay to secure U.S. Dollars. If this spikes, a global dollar shortage is occurring, which will temporarily crush gold mining equities regardless of the U.S. deficit.
Gold Priced in Euros/Yen (XAU/EUR, XAU/JPY): If gold is flat or down in USD terms, but breaking out to all-time highs in Euro and Yen terms, it confirms your currency debasement thesis is working globally, and the U.S. Dollar price will eventually catch up. [1]

Now that the miners have had a downturn it creates an environment were M&A can increase.

I never experience a stock of mine being bought out by a bigger miner.

What is the most profitable way to play a M&A process?

Do you keep the stock until it changes its ticker name to the bigger miner, and then sell your shares?
Or do you sell it a few days/weeks before the ticker symbol changes?

If I have a NPV calculation of the small miner, and it gets bought out lower than my calculation then I suppose you left money on the table.

Because the bigger-miner needs to buy it below NPV, otherwise there is "nothing in it for them". But, it also depends on strategy making valuing this difficult, does the merger add even more value than the single-miner without merger.

At the other hand they can decide the shareprice it gets bought at before the ticker change. Thus the difference in time of anouncemet and ticker change is the time for the market to make the price converge to that takeover-pricenumber.

In trying to learn how value Prospect Generators I went into the Rule Classroom. There there is a short lecture on prospect generators. And Rick mentions that there is only one model. He teaches it in the last 4 minutes of the video.

I don't understand some terminologies though, and maybe someone can help me out.

Here is the transcription of the last 4 minutes of the video:

How do you value them?
There is only one model.
When I evaluate a royalty company, I evaluate a royalty company by using a model that, is not a really good model.

But it is the best model in the world because it is the only model that exists.

Rick: I look at third party expenditures on projects that I generated and control X(mulitplied by) the working interest in my carried interest.
Example: Albert generated a project, and Rick is farming into it. And Rick is going to spend 10Million dollars on it. And you have a 30% “carry” in it.

Rick says then that that 3 Million dollars, that carried expenditure on your behalf is synthetic revenue. And Rick adds all third party expenditures on all the projects that he has generated. And that becomes his revenue. All be it synthetic revenue.

It is important that you burden it. That you burden those expenditures with the percentage that you carry. And I juxta-pose that number, my synthetic revenue against my actual costs.
Did it cost me 3 Million dollars a year? To generate 6 Million dollars a year in synthetic revenue? 
In that case I have synthetic profits. These profits are extremely synthetic because you can’t bank them. You can’t spend them. But what they are is the very best method for understanding the amount of leverage that you are enjoying.

It is precisely the amount of money that is being spent on your behalf. That raises or lowers the probability that you will enjoy an economic success and/or a take-over.

It is all about capital efficiency.
The prospect generator model does not work if the generator is capital inefficient. It does not work if there is no synthetic revenue, but there are all kinds of real expenses. He has had examples where the amount of third party expenditures that they generated was dwarfed, by the amount of real expenditures that they did generate, mainly in G&A fancy salaries.

I wrote in Bold the terminologies that I don't understand.
- What is: the working interest in my carried interest?
- What is "carry" in it?
- How do you burden the expenditures?
- Is juxta-pose the expenditures with synthetic revenue = revenue minus expenditures? Or does it mean something different?

Today Seabridge announced an unsecured short-term loan facility of up to US$100 million from an unnamed “strategic investor.” The stated purpose is to support 2026 summer work programs at KSM (roads, geotechnical, metallurgical and environmental data collection). With this in mind, two main interpretations could follow:
Interpretation A (More Cautious View):
The announcement may signal that the JV is taking longer than expected. In advanced negotiations with a major partner, introducing new debt from another strategic investor could be seen as unusual or even risky if not fully coordinated. Why announce a credit line if they already have enough cash for the planned work and have no immediate intention to draw it? This could be interpreted by the market as subtle pressure on the JV partner or as preparation for further delays, which might weigh on the share price in the short term.
Interpretation B (Strategic/Constructive View):
This is a smart tactical move by management. The facility provides a low-dilution liquidity backstop and strengthens Seabridge’s negotiating position with the preferred JV partner (“we can keep advancing KSM with or without you right now”). It allows the company to maintain full momentum on critical 2026 de-risking activities without slowing down. Announcing it (while emphasizing no draw yet) sends a positive signal to the broader market: Seabridge has access to patient strategic capital and remains well-funded.

text: Last week there was a short thread here about the valuation of uranium companies, probably triggered by the latest RIM newsletter. I stated that last time I checked many companies were generously valued at the current uranium price. Today I dug a little deeper. Starting at Nexgen, the current mkt cap is 6.2B USD, cash and debt are of a similar magnitude, EV around 6B USD. Attached is a view on updated (2023) numbers from the FS (2021) from the NXE website under assets → arrow. They state that the NPV of Arrow at $90 USD/lb is 5.84B CAD, which translates to 4.2B USD. So despite the fact that the company has just started construction, does not have full funding arranged yet, and cash flow is 4 years out, the company is already valued at 1.4 times NPV. There is upside in resource conversion (~80 Mlbs) and in their early stage PCE project. This looks to me to be more of a growth play than a value play. If you believe that the uranium price will be at $200 in two years, then the NPV of Arrow increases (using rough linear extrapolation) to 1.22 B USD in which case NXE is valued at 0.5 times NPV. I see something similar at Paladin. They have production from Langer Heinrich, which is high cost, mid scale, limited margin, and they have PLS which is low cost, large scale but they need to get the permit, spend 900 M USD on construction and production is 4-5 years out. I believe Paladin is trading around 1.1 times its NPV at current commodity prices. In a high uranium price environment they seem to have more room to grow than Nexgen. Am I overlooking something important? Any alternative views or maybe corrections would be very helpful.
